title: How do you implement health checks in an ASP.NET Core service?
description: Liveness vs readiness probes, checking dependencies safely, and what orchestrators do with them.

data.text: **Question:** How do you implement health checks in an ASP.NET Core service?

Add the health-checks middleware (`AddHealthChecks().AddCheck<T>()`, `MapHealthChecks("/health")`) and expose **two endpoints with different meanings**: **liveness** answers 'is this process running and not deadlocked' (self-only, never checks dependencies — a failing database must not restart every pod), and **readiness** answers 'should this instance receive traffic' (checks DB, cache, broker, disk). Kubernetes/load balancers/orchestrators route on readiness and restart on liveness; failing checks return 503 with a minimal body.

**The two (three) probes:**
- **Liveness** — process health: no dependency checks. If it fails, restart helps (deadlock, stuck static state)
- **Readiness** — traffic permission: DB reachable, config loaded, migration applied, broker connected. Fail → take out of rotation; recovery → put back in. Restart does *not* fix a down database, so never conflate the two
- **Startup probe** — long grace period for slow warm-up (JIT, migrations) before liveness kicks in, so healthy-but-slow instances aren't restarted in a loop

**Design points:**
- Each check implements `IHealthCheck`: return `HealthCheckResult.Healthy/Degraded/Unhealthy` with data (e.g. latency, pending migrations)
- Tag checks (`"db"`, `"queue"`) and expose tagged endpoints: `/health/ready?check=db` vs `/health/live`
- Response writer: minimal body for orchestrators (`Results.Ok`/`ServiceUnavailable`) — don't leak exception details (a public `/health` is reconnaissance gold)
- **Timeouts:** checks run with a per-check timeout (set it to a few seconds, not the 30s default); a hung dependency must flip to Unhealthy, not hang the probe
- **Frequency & cost:** readiness may be polled every 5–10 s — checking a remote service each time multiplies load; use caching/`HealthCheckRegistration` intervals, and make checks cheap (SELECT 1, not a full query)
- `Predicate` to exclude noisy checks from an endpoint
- Degraded is a real state: report it (still serving, but lossy) and alert on it
- Wire results to telemetry: log transitions + OpenTelemetry metrics on probe outcomes

data.title: Separate liveness and readiness endpoints

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- The liveness-vs-readiness distinction — the single most common follow-up
- Knowing a failing dependency must fail readiness, not trigger restarts
- Cost/timeout awareness: probes are frequent and must be cheap
- Security: health responses shouldn't expose internals

items: One endpoint for both liveness and readiness — a database blip restarts every pod (thundering herd on recovery)
Health checks that run heavy queries every few seconds
No timeouts — a hung dependency makes probes hang and the orchestrator guesses
Exposing exception messages/SQL on a publicly reachable /health
Forgetting startup probes — slow migrations cause a restart loop
Marking readiness healthy while the migration step hasn't run yet
Why shouldn't the liveness probe check the database?
How do you handle a dependency that's down for an hour — restart or shed traffic?
How would you add a custom check for 'all migrations applied'?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Liveness = restart-worthy process failure; readiness = traffic-worthy dependencies
Tag checks and map them to /health/live and /health/ready
Cheap checks, strict timeouts, minimal responses
Startup probe absorbs slow warm-up before liveness applies
data.takeaway: Separate the questions 'should we restart it?' from 'should we send it traffic?' — conflating them turns outages into restart storms.
